LIVE ARTIFACT
The automated Navier--Stokes manuscript at workspaces/VSC-workspaces/navier-stokes. Preserve the settled datum-generated whole-terminal compatible-intersection theorem and every formal claim, label, hypothesis, citation, and distinction unless a separate mathematical audit requires a correction.

WHOLE-PAPER MOVEMENT FIXED BY THOMAS
1. State Fefferman's whole-space problem, its datum class, the equation, the global smoothness and energy target, one maximal classical history, and the target T_*=infinity. Stop once the finite alternative is visible.
2. Assume a finite last time and enter the perfectly stretching vortex directly. Develop the one-fluid stretching, transverse narrowing, pressure, and viscosity picture; separate persistent-material and recruited-core readings; connect the scene to global critical L3 escape, scaling, the half-derivative critical height H, and infinitely many first-passage levels before T_*. Let that finite-time escape force the temporal derivative Tower by repeated integration. Derive the pressure-complete mixed jet from the same equation.
3. Differentiate the critical-height identity and show how viscosity exposes higher spatial energies inside the same temporal rows. Develop the central reversal: a singularity asks every fixed temporal response to lose critical control, while a bounded completed row reaches stronger spatial Sobolev regularity. Display the temporal/spatial table, derive the Sobolev column, form finite adjacent rectangles, and state the whole-terminal estimate and compatible intersection once.
4. Apply the intersection. Project an arbitrary finite temporal-spatial coordinate and derive the classical mixed estimates. Return to the low rectangles to give critical height a finite roof, end the Zeno ladder, and close separately the persistent-material, exact-centering, and recruited-core vortex readings. Construct the common H-infinity endpoint, continue the same history, and contradict finite maximality.
5. Develop genuine consequences: a finite vorticity sum across infinitely many dyadic scales, the L3 endpoint seen from the opposite side, and the exact difference between the viscous Navier--Stokes Tower and a distinct Euler history.
Appendices. Keep local construction, historical estimates, expanded derivative/rectangle calculus, compatibility, pressure jet, and endpoint gluing out of the causal body. Make the technical prose readable and direct, but do not turn the appendices back into a second narrative paper.

VOICE AND READER MOVEMENT
Enter the live idea without institutional staging. Speak with the mathematical reader. Explain the consequence that creates each next definition or estimate. Elaborate where the reader needs the causal step. Do not announce what a section will do, catalogue machinery, brand elementary quantities, defend the manuscript's organization, narrate proof status, or close a passage by repeating everything just proved. A question may organize the reasoning internally, but do not force rhetorical questions into the prose. Keep one actual fluid history in view. Preserve the distinction V_n=partial_t^n u versus material acceleration D_tu, and do not infer pointwise velocity blow-up from critical-height divergence alone.

ENDING
The body must land on the contradiction: the lowest rectangles block the critical escape and vortex concentration; the full intersection gives one smooth terminal value; local uniqueness continues the same history beyond T_*; hence T_* is infinite. Technical compatibility and jet assembly remain in the appendix.

The Three-Dimensional Navier–Stokes Regularity
                  Problem
                                  Thomas Birnie
                                  August 16, 2026


                                       Abstract
    We prove global existence and smoothness for the unforced three-dimensional
incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on R3 , for every viscosity ν > 0 and every
divergence-free Schwartz initial velocity. Assume that the maximal classical time T∗ is
finite. The energy identity still bounds kinetic energy, but continuation theory forces
both the critical L3 norm and the half-derivative height
                                       1
                                 H(t) = ∥Λ1/2 u(t)∥22
                                       2
to escape every finite bound. A perfectly balanced stretching vortex gives that statement
its physical form: the same fluid would have to complete infinitely many critical-height
first passages before T∗ . Repeated integration in time then forces every fixed temporal
derivative of the velocity to lose the same critical control.
    Differentiating the original equation generates the complete time-and-space derivative
Tower, including the pressure response. Viscosity opens a spatial Sobolev column inside
each temporal row, so the very rows forced toward critical escape also contain stronger
spatial regularity. The whole-terminal rectangle estimate controls every finite piece of
this Tower, and compatibility places all of those pieces in one intersection belonging
to the same fluid history. Its lowest rectangles bound the L3 norm, critical height,
stretching action, and high-frequency tail; its higher rectangles give one common
terminal velocity in H ∞ . Local well-posedness and uniqueness continue that velocity
beyond T∗ , contradicting maximality. Thus T∗ = ∞, the velocity and normalized
pressure are smooth for all time, and kinetic energy remains bounded by its initial
value.

2.1    The perfectly balanced rip-cord vortex

fragmentation, and no off-centre drift. Each narrower state becomes the starting state for
the next stretch. The question is whether the same fluid can complete infinitely many such
tightenings before one finite time.

solution. It is the hardest clean version of the stretching picture: the geometry is kept
favourable to concentration, and the fixed-viscosity equation is left responsible for stopping
